claims.text: The GI application describes ringal weaving as an age-old craft of Uttarakhand, in which artisans weave a special species of dwarf ringal that grows in the area.

quotes.quote: Ringal weaving is a nifty art of Uttarakhand. It is an age old craft of Uttarakhand. The artisans use a special species of dwarf Ringal that grows in these areas to weave.

claims.text: The GI application says ringal is woven into baskets, bins, mats and other utility items that were intricately woven yet sturdy to look at.

quotes.quote: There are different verities of Ringal weaving in the form of baskets, bins, mats and other utility items that were intricately woven, yet sturdy to look at.

claims.text: Ringal is the thin, reed-like group of bamboo in Uttarakhand, sometimes called dwarf bamboo, as distinct from the thick bamboos.

quotes.quote: There are two broad groups of bamboo, thickbamboo and thin reed like bamboo (ringal).
Ringal is the small reed-like variety of bamboo (sometimes called dwarf bamboo)

claims.text: Ringal weavers are locally known as Rudiya or Rudia, while the artisans who make articles from thick bamboo are called Baruree.

quotes.quote: used by the ringal weavers (locally known as Rudiya) for making ringal based crafts and utility items
The communities that make articles from bamboo and ringal are called Baruree and Rudia, respectively.

claims.text: Ringaal weaving sustains many Rudia households in Uttarakhand, and the Rudia community works this mountain dwarf bamboo across Garhwal and Kumaon.

quotes.quote: Ringaal bamboo weaving sustains many Rudia households in Uttarakhand.
The Rudia community works this mountain dwarf bamboo across Garhwal and Kumaon.

claims.text: The GI application states that scheduled caste families of the region have retained ancient, traditional knowledge of ringal weaving since time immemorial.

quotes.quote: Among these forest resources, Ringal is the most beneficial of the livelihood resources particularly for the scheduled caste families of the region. These families have retained ancient as well as traditional knowledge of ringal weaving work since time immemorial.

claims.text: Sundriyal and Sundriyal report that the Rudia ringal artisans, mainly marginalised scheduled caste families who lacked land, have depended on the bamboo trade for centuries.

quotes.locator: p. 451, socio economic status of the artisans
quotes.quote: Rudias (ringal artisans) in the state was very poor, which mainly comprised highly marginalized scheduled caste families. They lacked land and other productive resources for their livelihood and therefore have been dependent on bamboo trade for centuries.

claims.text: PARI reports that making bamboo products has been a traditional occupation of Bajela men in Jaiti village, Pithoragarh district, but found just one bamboo weaver left among its people.

quotes.quote: Nain Ram Bajela sits on the roof of his home in Jaiti village of Munsiari tehsil, weaving baskets on a cold winter morning.
Life in these mountains of Pithoragarh district of Uttarakhand is tough, and people have limited livelihood options.
Making bamboo products has been a traditional occupation of the men of the Bajela caste here - but Nain Ram is the last bamboo weaver left among Jaiti's 580 people.

claims.text: A Voices of Rural India story says the ringal trade in Namik village has been rooted in the community for approximately 200 to 300 years, spanning 6 to 7 generations.

quotes.quote: Ringal trade is an age-old tradition in Namik, an occupation that has been rooted in the community for approximately 200-300 years, spanning 6-7 generations.

claims.text: Development Alternatives describes the ringal handicraft industry as the oldest small-scale industry of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, based on local human and natural resources.

quotes.quote: Ringal handicraft industry is the oldest small scale industry of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It is the only home scale industry which is based on local resources, both in terms of human and natural resources.

claims.text: A design study links ringaal work historically with the Rudia or Bedi community, a Scheduled Caste group central to village services yet constrained by limited land.

quotes.quote: historically linked with the Rudia/Bedi communi ty, a Scheduled Caste group central to village services yet constrained by limited land

claims.text: The Voices of Rural India writer from Namik says his family belongs to the Shilpkar community, a Scheduled Caste whose craft is often seen as lowly work.

quotes.quote: The other reason is that we belong to the Shilpkar community (Scheduled Caste), and casteism is still a major problem in our society.
The craft and trade of the Shilpkar community is often seen as lowly work by society.

claims.text: Farmers fetch ringal from the forest in October to November and weave the baskets in winter, when there is not much work in the fields.

quotes.quote: The farmers fetch the ringal Ringal from the forest in October to November and weave the baskets in the winter when there is not much work in fields.

claims.text: Ringal is collected throughout the year for a variety of purposes, and only well-formed culms of 2 to 3 cm diameter are preferred for harvesting.

quotes.quote: Ringal is collected throughout the year for a variety of purposes. Only well -formed culm of 2-3 cm diameter is preferred for harvesting.

claims.text: Ringal is harvested with general household tools, and the cut is made up to 10 to 15 cm above the ground to help it re-sprout the next year.

quotes.quote: General household tools are used for harvesting. A cut is made up to 10- 15 cm above the ground, which helps to facilitate re-sprouting next year.

claims.text: About 5 to 8 conical ghida baskets can be made from the 30 kg of culms that one person collects in a daylong visit.

quotes.quote: About 5-8 Ghidas can be prepared by 30 kg culms collected in a daylong visit by a person.
An average of 8- 10 sticks is used for preparing conical baskets (Ghida) of average height.

claims.text: Sundriyal and Sundriyal found that collecting ringal takes between 6 hours and 2 days, while artisans spend 2 to 6 hours collecting bamboo.

quotes.quote: The artisans spend 2 to 6 hours for collection of bamboo, while it takes between 6 hours to 2 days for collection of ringal.

claims.text: In the villages of one design study, women joined forest trips, cleaned culms and prepared strips, while men did most of the weaving.

quotes.quote: In these sites, men undertook most weaving. Women joined forest trips, cleaned culms, prepared strips, and assisted with finishing and orders.
Women often join forest trips, carry loads, clean culms, and prepare strips. Men do most weaving.

claims.text: The GI application lists traditional processing as light peeling of the bark, drying for 3 to 4 days in the sun or a kitchen corner, division into 4 to 12 parts, and weaving.

quotes.quote: Traditional processing methods involve exposing the bark (light peeling); drying for 3- 4 days in sun or kitchen corner; division in 4- 12 parts according to the requirements; and weaving or crafting domestic implements.

claims.text: A Namik craftsman's account has ringal cut from the van panchayat forest with a darati, cut at once into thin outer strips called putra, and then dried in the sun.

quotes.locator: section The craft of Ringal weaving
quotes.quote: First, the Ringal has to be cut from the forest of our Van Panchayat using a darati. Immediately after, it is skilfully and precisely cut into strips called putra (the thin outer layer of the Ringal). These are then dried in the sun
how they held the darati (a metal tool used for cutting wood, grass, and Ringal)

claims.text: Project FUEL describes the first step as cutting, cleaning and splitting the ringaal with a sickle, after which a mallet flattens the pieces and they are cleaned again.

quotes.quote: The first step to make a Ringaal product is to cut, clean and split the bamboo using a sickle. After this, the artisan uses a mallet to flatten down the pieces. It is then again cleaned to smoothen the surface.

claims.text: The whole ringal is split into small strips to suit the product, its excess fibre is removed, and the ringal is split in different widths for the warp and the weft.

quotes.quote: The whole Ringal is split into small strips as per the product to be made. The excess fibre of Ringal splits are removed before weaving the basket. Artisan makes sure to split the Ringal in different widths for warp and weft.

claims.text: Each culm splits into 4 to 8 longitudinal strips or more, depending on the basket's shape and size and the culm's thickness, and is then scraped to smooth the edges and even the thickness.

quotes.quote: Each culm splits into 4 -8 longitudinal strips and sometimes more depending upon the shape and size of the basket and the culm's thickness. This is then scraped to smoothen the edges and for having uniform thickness especially at the nodes.

claims.text: A weaver in Jaiti cuts ringal into thin strips with a curved knife that he calls a baransh in his Pahadi language, PARI reports.

quotes.quote: He cuts the ringal or pahadi ringal, a Himalayan species of bamboo, into thin strips with a curved knife that he calls a 'baransh' in his Pahadi language.

claims.text: The GI application lists the khurpi, a knife to cut ringal into strips and peel its outer layer, and a cutter to cut the bamboo to the sizes needed.

quotes.quote: Khurpi: Knife to cut into strips and peel the outer layer. Cutter: Used to cut the bamboo into required sizes.

claims.text: Ringaal basketry is careful and tool-light: makers remove nodes, split culms and weave at floor level, sometimes using their toes for grip.

quotes.quote: Ringaal basketry is careful and tool-light. Makers remove nodes, split culms, and weave at floor level, sometimes using toes for grip.

claims.text: Makers split the culm, thin the strips with a knife, bind a base, lift the sides and fit the rim, pausing to sun-dry parts to reduce warping.

quotes.quote: split the culm, thin strips with a knife, bind a base, lift the sides, and fit the rim. They pause to sundry parts to reduce warp.

claims.text: To weave a basket, thick wide strips are first laid to make the base, thin strips are woven over them, and the side walls are then raised with added strips.

quotes.quote: The thick wide strips are first placed to make the base. Thin strips are weaved by overlapping the base strips. Once the base is formed, the side walls are increased by adding the additional Ringal strips.

claims.text: Once the weave reaches the required height, the rim is sandwiched between two thick ringal splits that interlock the border.

quotes.quote: Once the weave is attained required height, the rim is sandwiched with two thick Ringal splits to interlock the border.

claims.text: To prepare the base, twelve splits are laid out in a square open weave, then bent upright and crossed over diagonally to form the wall.

quotes.quote: To prepare the base, twelve bamboo splits are laid out to form a square open weave. The splits are then bent vertically and crossed over to lie diagonally to form the wall.

claims.text: For winnows, a long ringal pole is split into wide thin splits; slightly tender splits are used directly, and dried splits are soaked in water to regain moisture.

quotes.quote: Lengthy Ringal pole is split into wide thin splits. Slightly tender Ringal splits are directly used for winnow weaving. In case if the Ringal splits are dried, they are soaked in water before weaving to regain moisture.

claims.text: A winnow is woven by arranging ringal strips criss-cross with a small ringal stick, cutting away the extra edges and tying a tender stick on the edge for reinforcement.

quotes.quote: Winnow weaving process is done by arranging the Ringal strips in criss-cross manner with the help of small Ringal stick. Once the weaving is completed, the extra edges are cut and removed. A small tender stick is tied on the edge of the winnow to give reinforcement.

claims.text: After weaving, ringaal baskets are coated and smoke-cured, simple local treatments that deter pests, moisture, insects and fungus.

quotes.quote: After weaving, baskets are coated and smokecured to deter pests and moisture.
For protection, they smoke-cure and use simple local coatings against insects and fungus

claims.text: One maker recalled that making a kandi was quite time-consuming, taking him an entire day for one basket.

quotes.quote: The process of making a kandi was quite time-consuming. It would take me an entire day to make one kandi.

claims.text: Artisans in a design study described long, risky harvest trips for ringaal on steep, narrow forest trails, where slips and animal encounters are common.

quotes.quote: Findings show long and risky harvest trips, basic tools, and uneven product quality.
Artisans described difficult harvests. Trails are steep and narrow, with night halts in the forest when needed. Slips and animal encounters are common.

claims.text: Among the artisans studied, cuts, splinters, and back and wrist pain were common, linked to floor-level postures and repetitive splitting and weaving.

quotes.quote: Work health and safety concerns were widespread. Cuts, splinters, and back and wrist pain were common, linked to floor-level postures and repetitive splitting and weaving.
Common harms include cuts and musculoskeletal pain from floor-level postures and repetitive splitting and weaving.

claims.text: In the workshops studied, knife work produced cuts and punctures, cutting and pounding released fine splinters that risked eye injuries, and hammering raised noise.

quotes.quote: Risks observed in workshops were clear and recurring across sites.
Cutting and pounding released fine splinters; bright, even light and safety glasses with side shields reduced eye injuries.
Hammering raised noise; earplugs and basic tool maintenance reduced exposure.

claims.text: Ringaal products are generally green, the natural colour of the bamboo; for decoration the inner splits are blackened with fire, and pink or yellow come from dyeing.

quotes.locator: How Ringaal craft products are made colourful
quotes.quote: The products are generally green in colour, owing to the natural colour of bamboo. To make the products decorative, the inner splits are blackened using fire. Other colours like pink or yellow are obtained by dying them.

claims.text: To decorate a supa, a Namik craftsman blackens ringal in the smoke of burning bark of the sauda tree, a species of uttis or alder.

quotes.locator: section The craft of Ringal weaving
quotes.quote: The work of decorating a supa is extremely labour-intensive and time-consuming. For this, first, the bark of the sauda tree, a species of the Uttis (Alder) tree, is burned, and the Ringal is blackened with its smoke.

claims.text: Artisans make patterns of dark and light contrast on a product's outer surface by selecting and inserting darker and lighter shades of ringal splits.

quotes.quote: Artisan scholarly weaves the basket and many crafts to obtain dark and lighter contrast on the outer surface of the product by selecting and inserting darker and lighter shades of Ringal
Finished pieces show patterns that play the inner-outer colour contrast of ringaal

claims.text: The GI application says most ringal products are roughly finished, with sharp edges and non-uniform colour and texture, as natural, eco-friendly products.

quotes.quote: Most of the products prepared by ringal are roughly finished with sharp edges, non- uniform in colour and texture as a natural and eco-friendly product.

claims.text: A design study records changeras as dome-shaped grain stores.

quotes.quote: Changeras are dome-shaped grain stores.

claims.text: Dry ringal sticks serve as cooking fuel, and ringal is also made into decorative items and kalam, ink pens that local astrologers use to write horoscopes.

quotes.quote: Dry sticks as fuel wood for cooking purposes; decorative items, and 'Kalam' (ink pen) used by local astrologers for writing horoscope.

claims.text: The GI application calls slightly conical ringal baskets solta or ghida, their size and shape varying with use, such as carrying water, food to fields or bulky material.

quotes.quote: Slightly conical shaped baskets are called 'Solta' or 'Ghida'. The size and shape of 'Ghida' or 'Solta' varies according to usage requirement such as carriage of water
carriage of bulky material, carriage of food to fields and pasture lands, storage purposes and collection of fruits

claims.text: The soulta, a basket for carrying grass, cow-dung cakes and firewood, has a hexagonal weave that makes it sturdy with minimal use of splits.

quotes.locator: Soulta - a type of Ringaal basket
quotes.quote: The artisan here is making soulta, a kind of basket that is used to carry grass, cow dung cakes and firewood. The hexagonal weave of the basket makes it sturdy with minimal use of bamboo splits.

claims.text: Woven ringal articles include the suppa winnower for grain, the moreta mat laid on earthen floors for sitting and drying grain, and the bhwanu broom.

quotes.quote: Various articles such as 'Suppa' (winnower) for winnowing of grains; 'Moreta' (mat) laid down on the earthen floor for sitting purposes and for drying grains and edible items; 'Bhwanu' (broom) for sweeping and cleaning floors.

claims.text: Ringal baskets carry livestock dung, manure, fuel wood, forest produce, fodder, grass, rations and clothes for washing, and vary in shape and capacity with their use.

quotes.quote: Weaving of various kinds of baskets and other articles form the major use of ringal among the Himalayan community for carrying livestock dung, manure, fuel wood and other forest produce, fodder, grass, ration, and clothes for washing. These vary in shape and capacity according to the use.

claims.text: A dense cylindrical basket is called kandi or kanda in Kumaon and ghilda in Garhwal, and women carry farm and forest loads in it.

quotes.quote: In Kumaon a dense cylinder is kandi or kanda; in Garhwal it is ghilda. Women carry farm and forest loads in these.

claims.text: Garhwal also has a three-sided ghilda for carrying elders and children to hill temples.

quotes.quote: Garhwal also has a three-sided ghilda for carrying elders and children to hill temples.

claims.text: The choura or jhuger, a round sleeping basket for a newborn baby, is made from Dendrocalamus somdevae or H. falconeri.

quotes.quote: Round sleeping basket Choura (Jhuger) D. somdevae, H. falconeri For sleeping of newly born baby

claims.text: In Namik, ringal is made into daliya storage baskets, moshta floor mats, supa winnowers, brooms and dokkas, baskets carried on the back for grass and dung.

quotes.quote: Ringal is used to make daliya (big baskets for storing goods and food), moshta (floor mats), supa (winnowing basket) for cleaning grains like lentils and rice, making brooms, and dokkas (a type of basket carried on the back for carrying grass and dung).
Ringal trade is an age-old tradition in Namik

claims.text: Newer ringaal lines include flower vases, dustbins, kandi baskets for fruit and vegetables, flower and prasad baskets, decorative bowls, small huts, display cups and kettles, and trays.

quotes.quote: Newer lines include flower vases, dustbins, kandi baskets for fruit and vegetables, flower baskets, prasad baskets, decorative bowls, small huts, display cups and kettles, and trays

claims.text: The GI application says dev ringal is used for puja purposes on spiritual yatras to Badrinath, Kedarnath and Nandadevi, and for baskets carrying puja utensils.

quotes.quote: The artisans use a special species of Ringal mximum Dev Ringal for puja purpose in various spiritual yatra in Badrinath, Kedarnath, Nandadevi
Prayer purpose, Tissue paper case, Mobile case, carrying Puja utensils in Dev Ringal

claims.text: Video Volunteers reports that the shrine and umbrella devotees carry to temples at major festivals are made from ringal, which is even mentioned in certain prayers.

quotes.quote: During the major festivals, the shrine and umbrella carried by the devotees to the temples is made from ringal, and it is even mentioned in certain prayers and scriptures.

claims.text: The GI application says women artisans have developed ringal rakhis for the Raksha Bandhan festival, which are in high demand in cities.

quotes.quote: Rakhi A variety of rakhi at the time of Rakshabandhan festival has developed by women artisans A innovative initiative is much appreciated in the city area with high demand as natural and unique product.

claims.text: In Munsiari block, some ringal baskets with handles and lids are used to carry food, particularly when young women leave for their marital homes.

quotes.quote: Some, with handles and lids, are also used to carry food, particularly when young women leave for their marital homes.
Fortunately, there's some demand for his products across Munsiari block

claims.text: The GI application says ringal is flexible and durable, and that products made from it can last up to 20 years.

quotes.quote: Ringal is a flexible, durable Ringal products made from it can last up to 20 years.

quotes.quote: The life duration of Ringal is nearly 20- 25 years and due to this the product made by Ringal is very popular for their long durability.

claims.text: A Millennium Post column says ringal products are tough and durable and last for at least 20 to 25 years.

quotes.quote: Ringal products are tough, durable and last for at least 20-25 years.

quotes.quote: January 10, 2011 | By: Luxmi Nautiyal
found in abundance in the higher mountain areas of the Garhwal region of Uttarakhand, where Luxmi lives

quotes.quote: The most important characteristic of Ringal is that, it is nearly water resistance in comparison to the Bamboo, and Ringal much survive in the snow fall area in upper Himalayan region

claims.text: Despite plastic and metal substitutes, households keep buying ringaal because it is light, repairable, comfortable to carry and suited to hill work.

quotes.quote: Despite plastic and metal substitutes, households continue to buy ringaal because it is light, repairable, and suited to hill work
Yet ringaal endures because it is light, easy to repair, and comfortable to carry

lede.text: The GI application describes ringal weaving as an age-old craft of Uttarakhand, in which a special species of dwarf ringal, a thin reed-like bamboo, is woven into baskets, bins, mats and other utility items.

Its weavers are known as Rudiya or Rudia, whom Sundriyal and Sundriyal describe as mainly marginalised scheduled caste families, and the GI application names Chamoli, Bageshwar, Pithoragarh, Almora and Rudraprayag among the places where ringal weaving gives a livelihood.
The GI application names four ringal species, and elsewhere five, and sources differ on which species is dev ringal and which weavers use most.
Uttarakhand Ringal Craft is registered as a geographical indication under application 652, with certificate number 391 dated 14 September 2021.

sentences.text: The GI application states that scheduled caste families of the region have retained ancient, traditional knowledge of ringal weaving since time immemorial.
Walton's 1911 Almora gazetteer names basket and matting making from ringal bamboo, with hemp and wool weaving, as the district's only industries of importance besides tea-making.

Sundriyal and Sundriyal report that the Rudia ringal artisans, who lacked land, have depended on the bamboo trade for centuries, and a design study links the work historically with the Rudia or Bedi community.

In Jaiti village of Pithoragarh district, making bamboo products has been a traditional occupation of the men of the Bajela caste, PARI reports, though it found just one bamboo weaver left among the village's people.
A Voices of Rural India story says the ringal trade in Namik village has been rooted in the community for approximately 200 to 300 years.
Development Alternatives describes the ringal handicraft industry as the oldest small-scale industry of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh.
Farmers fetch ringal from the forest in October to November and weave the baskets in winter, when there is not much work in the fields, although ringal is also collected throughout the year.
Only well-formed culms of 2 to 3 cm diameter are preferred, and the cut is made up to 10 to 15 cm above the ground to help the plant re-sprout the next year.

The GI application lists light peeling of the bark, drying for 3 to 4 days, division into 4 to 12 parts and weaving, while a Namik craftsman's account has the strips cut first and then dried in the sun.
Each culm splits into 4 to 8 longitudinal strips or more, which are scraped to even thickness, and separate strips are prepared for the warp and the weft.
Thick wide strips are first laid to make the base, the side walls are raised with added strips, and the rim is sandwiched between two thick ringal splits.
After weaving, ringaal baskets are coated and smoke-cured to deter pests, moisture, insects and fungus.
Collecting ringal takes between 6 hours and 2 days, and about 30 kg of culms gathered in a daylong visit makes about 5 to 8 ghida baskets.

Sources differ on how long ringal products last: up to 20 years or nearly 20 to 25 years in the GI application, at least 20 to 25 years in a Millennium Post column, and six to seven years in a 2011 Video Volunteers account.
Households keep buying ringaal despite plastic and metal substitutes because it is light, repairable and suited to hill work.
Large baskets are harnessed to the back with rope of dholan and bhang, and in the articles Sundriyal and Joshi surveyed, some artisans tied baskets with ghingaroo stems.
Ringal culms are woven into mats and baskets, and the green leaves are used as fodder for animals.
Thamnocalamus spathiflorus was commonly used to cover the roofs of grassy houses and to make hookah pipes and walking sticks.

For marginalised hill-area villages, the GI application names four ringal species of the Poaceae family: Himalayacalamus falconeri, Chimnobambusa jaunsarensis, Drepanostachyum falcatum and Thamnocalamus spathiflorus.
Sundriyal and Sundriyal record ghad ringal at 1500 to 2100 meters, jumra ringal at 2100 to 2700 meters, dev ringal at 1900 to 2750 meters and thaam ringal at 2500 to 3500 meters.
Sources differ on whether dev ringal is Himalayacalamus or Thamnocalamus falconeri, or Thamnocalamus spathiflorus.

They also differ on which species weavers use most: Chimnobambusa jaunsarensis in one passage of the GI application, dev ringal in Sundriyal and Sundriyal, and Drepanostachyum falcatum at lower altitudes in another passage.
Sources differ on ringal's height: an average of 12 ft for its culms in one source, 5 to 8 meters in a Voices of Rural India story, and 2 to 3.5 m for Arundinaria falcata in Flora of Pakistan.
The board gives ringal an average flowering cycle of about 30 years, and a new crop emerges around August to September and becomes flexible, strong and ready to use from February to March.

Ringal grows on steep mountain slopes in the Garhwal and Kumaon hills, generally as the understorey of oak and rhododendron forests, and sources differ on its altitude, from 1800 to 2400 m in one account to 1,000 to 2,000 metres or 1200 to 3600 meters in others.
Most bamboo and ringal habitats fall under reserve forest, civil soyam and van panchayat village forest areas.

A study published in 2011 found nearly 93% of ringal artisans collecting ringal directly from forests, mainly van panchayat forests, and sources differ on whether villagers collect it free or on nominal charges for domestic needs.
Where collection of ringal was banned, the raw material was collected illegally, and most ringal-growing areas have shrunk to far-flung places away from villages.
A Voices of Rural India story says ringal helps prevent landslides, and Katiyar recommends planting Arundinaria falconeri on roadsides and slopes to control landslides and soil erosion.

Sugandh Uttarapath Kisan Swayat Sahkarita applied on 27 May 2019 to register Uttarakhand Ringal Craft as a geographical indication, and the registry records certificate number 391 dated 14 September 2021.
The application was advertised in Geographical Indications Journal 138, dated 30 June 2020, and the registry's table of authorised users numbers its entries up to 120.
A study published in 2011 found 75% of ringal artisan families below the poverty line and Scheduled Caste, and 55% of ringal artisans earning Rs. 2000 to 4000 a month.
Sources differ on the number of artisan villages: as many as 451 bamboo artisan villages in a 2011 study, and over 460 villages depending on bamboo and ringal in 2005 board records.
The same 2011 study estimated selling prices 10 to 30% higher in towns, but artisans preferred to sell in villages to avoid transport costs.
Ringaal sales moved through village traders, government emporia, NGO purchases and occasional bulk civic orders, with prices set from material and time and then negotiated by buyer type.
Artisans described youth moving out and plastic and metal ware spreading, and a Millennium Post column says ringal weaving is on the verge of extinction.
Sundriyal and Joshi's 2015 case study gives market costs from Rs. 40 to 50 for a big kandi to Rs. 700 to 800 for a moste, and a 2011 Video Volunteers account priced a ringal basket at Rs. 50.
Artisans make patterns of dark and light contrast by selecting and inserting darker and lighter shades of ringal splits.

Ringaal products are generally green, and for decoration the inner splits are blackened with fire or, in one Namik craftsman's account, with the smoke of burning sauda bark, while pink or yellow come from dyeing.

The GI application calls slightly conical baskets solta or ghida, while a design study describes the soulta as a cylinder with a hexagon weave, and a dense cylindrical basket is called kandi or kanda in Kumaon and ghilda in Garhwal.
Woven ringal articles include the suppa winnower, the moreta mat laid on earthen floors and the bhwanu broom.
The GI application says dev ringal is used for puja purposes on spiritual yatras to Badrinath, Kedarnath and Nandadevi.
Newer ringaal lines include flower vases, dustbins, prasad baskets, decorative bowls and trays, and women artisans have developed ringal rakhis.
The GI application says most ringal products are roughly finished, with sharp edges and non-uniform colour and texture.
Artisans in a design study described long, risky harvest trips for ringaal on steep, narrow forest trails, where slips and animal encounters are common.
Among the artisans studied, cuts, splinters, and back and wrist pain were common, linked to floor-level postures and repetitive splitting and weaving.
In the workshops studied, cutting and pounding released fine splinters that risked eye injuries, and hammering raised noise.
